subject: 'United States' is not one eligibility rule — it is at least three, and they disagree
finding: Four US opportunities researched in this lane resolve the SAME student's case in materially different ways. Flattening any of them to eligible_countries=['United States'] destroys the distinction and will mislead students in both directions.

the_three_patterns.verbatim: 'Any student who is living in and attending their last year of secondary school in the US and its territories may apply, regardless of citizenship.' Plus: 'Students who are US citizens living abroad may also qualify.' And the exclusion: 'Students attending American schools abroad, but who are not US citizens, are not eligible.'
'Be a U.S. citizen residing in the United States, or a Permanent Resident of the United States residing in the United States, or be stationed overseas due to active U.S. military duty.'

the_three_patterns.pattern: RESIDENCE + SCHOOL + CITIZENSHIP/PR — all three required
the_three_patterns.verbatim: 'must currently be living in and attending high school in the U.S. AND must be U.S. citizens or permanent residents with a green card'

the_three_patterns.pattern: RESIDENCE ONLY, with an officially-named alternative for everyone else
the_three_patterns.verbatim: PRIMES is 'available only to students who reside in the United States'; 'International students are welcome to participate in CrowdMath'

worked_example: Take one concrete student — a Turkish citizen, in their final year at an American school in Istanbul. Regeneron STS: NOT eligible (explicitly excluded by name). Davidson: NOT eligible (not a citizen/PR). SIMR: NOT eligible (not in the US, not a citizen). MIT PRIMES: NOT eligible, but MIT itself points them to CrowdMath, where they ARE eligible. Now move the same student physically to a US high school: STS becomes eligible, Davidson and SIMR still are not. One country field cannot express any of this.
product_implication: ORYN's advisor will be asked exactly this question by exactly this kind of student — AGENTS.md names 'international students applying abroad' as a target segment. A single eligible_countries array cannot answer it, and worse, it answers confidently and wrongly. The honest minimum is to store the eligibility RULE TEXT alongside the country list, so the advisor can quote the operator rather than infer from a country tag.
recommendation: Do not attempt to normalise these four into a shared country representation. Where the rule is more than a country list, keep the verbatim sentence — every one of my records carries it in a *_verbatim field for this reason.

canonical_name: The Anson L. Clark Scholars Program
what_students_do_verbatim: Participants engage in 'hands-on practical research experience with outstanding and experienced faculty' and complete a research project report.
research_nature: GENUINE mentored university research with a required written report.
cohort_verbatim: 'twelve highly qualified rising high school seniors and recent high school graduates'
cohort_note: TWELVE PLACES. Among the most selective research programmes in the corpus — comparable in scarcity to RSI's 100 worldwide.
eligibility_verbatim: 'Applicants must be at least 17 years of age by the program start date, and should graduate in 2026 or 2027.'
citizenship_rule_verbatim: 'Must be a U.S. Citizen or Permanent Resident.'
CORRECTION_OF_A_CIRCULATING_CLAIM: Search results — including at least one commercial admissions-consulting blog — assert that Clark Scholars is 'open to both US and international high school students' and even advise international applicants to arrange their own visas. THE OFFICIAL PAGE SAYS THE OPPOSITE: 'Must be a U.S. Citizen or Permanent Resident.' I resolved the conflict from the operator's own eligibility page, not from the snippet. This is a concrete instance of why aggregator and consultancy content is discovery-only: acting on it would have sent an international student through a full application they cannot win.
stipend_verbatim: 'Upon completion of a successful research project report, the Scholar will receive a $750 stipend.'
cost_coverage: On-campus meals, room and board, and weekend activities provided. Travel to/from the programme, personal expenses and medical costs are NOT covered.
cost_note: No tuition; a $750 stipend is paid on completion. But travel is explicitly the student's own cost — a real expense that a bare 'free' label would hide.
deadline_note: NOT STATED on the official page. Secondary sources say the 2027 application opens in autumn 2026; that is NOT officially confirmed and no date is recorded.
unresolved: Official application deadline for the 2027 cycle.

subject: The US research pathway is effectively closed to students who are not in the US — with two specific exceptions
finding: Across every flagship US research programme researched in this lane, international students are excluded either by citizenship, by residence, or both. This is not one programme's policy; it is the shape of the whole tier.

evidence_table.rule: 'Must be a U.S. Citizen or Permanent Resident.'
'living in and attending high school in the U.S. AND must be U.S. citizens or permanent residents with a green card'
'a U.S. citizen residing in the United States, or a Permanent Resident… residing in the United States, or… stationed overseas due to active U.S. military duty'
'available only to students who reside in the United States'
evidence_table.open_to_international: NO — but MIT names the alternative itself

evidence_table.rule: Two-track: US applicants apply directly; international applicants must go through their own country's selecting agency, list unpublished
evidence_table.open_to_international: CONDITIONALLY — only if your country participates, and you must ask CEE whether it does

evidence_table.rule: 'living in and attending their last year of secondary school in the US and its territories… regardless of citizenship'
evidence_table.open_to_international: ONLY IF PHYSICALLY IN THE US — and explicitly NOT if at an American school abroad

evidence_table.rule: eligible_countries=['United States'] in the live corpus; official page silent on citizenship
NOT STATED on the page retrieved

the_two_exceptions: For a student outside the US, exactly two doors in this tier are actually open: (1) **CrowdMath** (CR1-053) — free, worldwide, no gate, and MIT PRIMES' own page directs international students there by name; (2) **RSI** (CR1-017), but only via a national agency whose existence must be confirmed country by country.
product_implication: AGENTS.md names the United States as the first target geography AND names 'international students applying abroad' as a core segment. Those two facts collide here. If ORYN surfaces the US research tier to a student in Türkiye without the eligibility rules attached, it will recommend a sequence of applications that student is structurally barred from — the most expensive possible failure mode in a product whose stated job is opportunity cost. The right behaviour is the pattern MIT itself models: name the closed door briefly, then hand over the open one.
recommendation: Any US research row surfaced to a non-US student must carry its citizenship/residence rule verbatim, and where an official alternative exists (PRIMES→CrowdMath) the record should link it.
